title: Why Prices End in .99 (And Why It Still Works on You)

spine.goal: Dave wants to prove that the .99 trick does not work on him and win back the $20 he bet Bob
spine.stakes: He spent $124.95 while his head said 'about ninety', he is out $20 and his pride, and his brain keeps rounding every price down
spine.central_question: Why does a pricing trick that everybody knows about still work on everybody, and who decides the last digit?
spine.loop_big: The exact price tag from the first second comes back in the last minute and the viewer (and Dave) finally read it as four hundred dollars
spine.loop_mid: Pause-and-guess: how many cents does a one-cent jump from $4.99 to $5.00 feel like to shoppers? (about twenty)
spine.villain: The pricing office that picks every last digit on purpose, helped by our own left-to-right brain (and by shoppers who punish honest prices)
spine.low_point: J.C. Penney tried honest round prices in 2012 and lost about four billion dollars of sales in a year; then the U.S. stopped making the penny and .99 survived anyway
spine.win: Dave says every price out loud rounded up, keeps a round running total, asks 'would I want it at the round price?', then wins the double-or-nothing rematch and gets $40 from Bob

youtube.title: Why Prices End in .99 (And Why It Still Works on You)
youtube.hook: You know $9.99 is ten dollars. Your brain still files it under nine. Here is where that one-penny trick came from, what it really costs you, and how Dave finally beat it.

sources: Thomas & Morwitz (New York University), 'Penny Wise and Pound Foolish: The Left-Digit Effect in Price Cognition', Journal of Consumer Research 32(1), June 2005 (effect only when the leftmost digit changes, e.g. $2.99 vs $3.00)

Lacetera, Pope & Sydnor, 'Heuristic Thinking and Limited Attention in the Car Market', American Economic Review, Aug 2012 (over 22 million used-car transactions; drops of about $150-$200 at each 10,000-mile mark; $210 at 80,000 miles)

List, Muir, Pope & Sun, 'Left-Digit Bias at Lyft', Review of Economic Studies (field experiment with 21 million passengers; about half of the demand response happens as the price drops below a dollar value; about $160M a year)

Strulov-Shlain (University of Chicago Booth), 'More than a Penny's Worth: Left-Digit Bias and Firm Pricing', Review of Economic Studies 90(5), 2023 (3,500 products, 25 U.S. chains; a 1-cent step from $4.99 to $5.00 acts like a 15-25 cent increase; retailers under-use it)

Levy, Lee, Chen, Kauffman & Bergen, 'Price Points and Price Rigidity', Review of Economics and Statistics, Nov 2011 (9 is the most frequent price ending in eight years of supermarket scanner data and in internet prices)
U.S. Patent 221,360 (4 Nov 1879), James Ritty and John Ritty, Dayton, Ohio: 'Cash Register and Indicator' (Ritty's Incorruptible Cashier); Smithsonian National Museum of American History

Cecil Adams, The Straight Dope, 'Why do prices end in .99?' (Melville Stone and cash-register legends; Chicago Daily News ads on microfilm: prices ending in 9 rare until well into the 1880s, common only after 1890)

Los Angeles Times, obituary of Dave Gold (April 2013) quoting his 2003 interview: wine at $1.02 or 98 cents 'never sold out', at 99 cents 'gone in no time'; first 99 Cents Only store 1982; chain closed all 371 stores in 2024
Apple press release, 5 May 2003: 'iTunes Music Store Sells Over One Million Songs in First Week' (99 cents a song)

NACS, 'Why Gas Is Priced Using Fractions of a Penny' (1930s gasoline taxes in fractions of a cent); EIA: U.S. motor gasoline consumption 8.9 million barrels a day in 2025 (x 42 gal x 365 = about 136 billion gallons; x $0.009 = about $1.2 billion)

U.S. Mint / Treasury: last circulating pennies struck in Philadelphia on 12 Nov 2025; unit cost 3.69 cents (FY2024). Common Cents Act: passed the House 14 Sept 2026 and the Senate 29 Sept 2026 (cash totals rounded to the nearest five cents; card payments not rounded)

J. C. Penney Company Form 10-K, fiscal 2012: net sales $12.985 billion, down 24.8% from $17.26 billion; 590 promotions in 2011 cut to 12 ('Fair and Square', round-number tags, Feb 2012); Ron Johnson dismissed 8 April 2013 after 17 months

beats.text: Look at this price tag for one second and be honest because your brain just filed it under three hundred something didn't it?
It's four hundred dollars and stores have run that one penny trick on you for over a century.
It works so well that one giant store quit it along with its coupons and lost four billion dollars in one year.
In ten minutes you'll see this exact tag again and your brain will finally read it right.
So meet Dave who just walked out of a store feeling very smart because he's sure this stuff only works on other people.
Dave says please. I know nine ninety nine is ten bucks and I'm not a child.
His neighbor Bob hears that and grins and says twenty dollars says you can't tell me what you just spent without looking at the receipt.
Dave thinks about the headphones and the lamp and the frying pan and the snacks and then he says easy. It was about ninety bucks.
The receipt says one hundred twenty four dollars and ninety five cents.
Dave didn't forget anything. His brain kept the first digit of every price and threw the rest away like a guy who reads the first word of your text and replies okay.
And before you laugh at Dave here's a real shelf tag from a real store. Is your gut saying three bucks or four?
Now try three at once. You've got three seconds so add these up in your head and no calculator.
If you got somewhere around ninety then congratulations because you're Dave. The real total is three cents short of a hundred.
So Dave is out twenty dollars and he wants to know how a trick this dumb beat him. The trail starts in an Ohio saloon in eighteen seventy nine.
Dave looks it up and the first story he finds is about a saloon owner in Dayton Ohio named James Ritty.
Ritty was sure his bartenders were pocketing the cash so in eighteen seventy nine he patented a machine he called the Incorruptible Cashier. You know it as the cash register.

And here's the legend. If your drink costs one round dollar the bartender can slide that bill straight into his pocket. But at ninety nine cents he has to open the drawer for your penny and the sale gets recorded.
It's a great story and it's all over the internet but nobody has ever found a shop owner from back then saying that's why he did it.
The second story stars a Chicago newspaper man named Melville Stone who sold his paper for one penny back when almost nobody in town carried pennies.
The tale goes that he talked local shops into pricing things one cent under the dollar so you'd get a penny back and spend it on his paper.
Cute right? Except a columnist dug through that paper's old ads on microfilm and prices ending in nine were rare until well into the eighteen eighties.
Dave says hold on. So I lost twenty bucks to a rumor?
Pretty much. Nobody really knows who started it. What we do know is why it never stopped and that part happens inside your head.
Dave still doesn't buy it so let's test your brain on something that isn't even a price. Look at the odometer on this used truck.
Ninety nine thousand miles feels a lot younger than a hundred thousand doesn't it? And that gap is one long weekend of driving.
Researchers went through millions of used car sales and a car sold just before a big round mileage number went for about two hundred dollars more than the same car just after it.
So in plain English you read from left to right and your brain decides how big a number is before your eyes reach the end. Scientists call it the left digit effect.

Two researchers at New York University tested it in two thousand five. Two ninety nine felt clearly cheaper to people than three dollars. But when the first digit stayed the same that one cent did almost nothing.
Dave does this with everything by the way. He is thirty nine years and eleven months old and he tells people he's thirty something.
Now guess with me. When a price climbs one single cent from four ninety nine to five dollars how many cents does that feel like to shoppers?
Put your number in the comments because the answer is coming in a minute. But first Dave finds a man who built a whole empire on those two little nines.
His name was Dave Gold and he ran his family's little liquor store in downtown Los Angeles.
Gold noticed something weird. When he put wine on sale for a dollar and two cents it just sat there and at ninety eight cents it sat there too.
But when he wrote ninety nine cents on the sign it was gone in no time. He called it a magic number.
Think about that. The wine sold better at ninety nine cents than at ninety eight. A higher price beat a lower one because of how it looked.
So in nineteen eighty two he opened a store where every single thing cost ninety nine cents and he called it Ninety Nine Cents Only.
It grew into hundreds of stores. And when his costs went up do you know what the new price was? It was ninety nine point nine nine cents.
And he wasn't the only one who knew. In two thousand three Steve Jobs opened a music store on your computer and he priced every song at ninety nine cents.
It sold a million songs in its first week.
Dave says okay so ninety nine sells. But who decides that my lamp costs nineteen ninety nine and not twenty?
Great question Dave. Because somebody does decide and that somebody has a spreadsheet.
Dave always pictured a price tag as a kind of accident. It isn't. Every big chain has a pricing office and choosing the last digit is somebody's actual job.
Economists checked eight years of prices from a big supermarket chain and nine was the most common last digit of them all.
And now you get your answer. A researcher at the University of Chicago tracked thousands of products across twenty five store chains.
When a price crosses from four ninety nine to five dollars shoppers react as if it went up by about twenty cents.
One penny hits your brain like twenty of them. So a store that knocks one cent off gets treated as if it gave you a real discount.
Do you want proof that it prints money? Economists ran an experiment on twenty one million riders of the ride app Lyft.
About half of everything a cheaper fare did happened at the exact moment the price slipped under a round dollar.
They worked out that ending fares in ninety nine could be worth around one hundred sixty million dollars a year to the company.
So that's who wins. It isn't one evil guy in a tower. It's a quiet office with a spreadsheet and it's using a glitch inside your own head.
And if you think one cent is the smallest thing they'd bother to shave off then wait until Dave pulls into a gas station.
Dave fills up his car and for the first time in his life he actually reads the sign.
Look at the tiny number sitting next to the price. That's nine tenths of a cent and there is no coin in your pocket for that.
Those fractions showed up on gas signs back in the nineteen thirties when gas taxes came in slivers of a cent and a whole penny was a big deal.
The taxes changed but the nine tenths never left. On one tank it costs you about a dime.
But Americans burn around one hundred thirty six billion gallons of gasoline a year.
So that invisible fraction adds up to more than a billion dollars every single year.
Dave says so I've been paying for a coin that doesn't even exist?
Now Dave has one hopeful thought. If we all hate being tricked then surely a store that stops doing it would win. One huge company tried exactly that.

beats.chapter: The Store That Told The Truth
beats.text: In twenty eleven the department store J C Penney hired a new boss named Ron Johnson. He was the man who had built the Apple Store.
Johnson looked at his new company and saw a mess. It had run five hundred ninety different sales in a single year.
So in twenty twelve he made a brave move. He cut the endless sales and he killed the coupons and he called the plan Fair and Square.
And the tags changed too. A price that used to end in ninety nine now ended in a nice honest zero.
Be honest with me. You'd love a store like that wouldn't you?
Shoppers walked away. Sales fell by about four billion dollars in one year which was a quarter of the whole business.
Johnson was out after seventeen months and the coupons came right back.
And that's the ugly truth Dave didn't want to hear. The stores aren't forcing this on us. We punish the honest price and we reward the pretty one.
But Dave had one last hope. Because in twenty twenty five the United States did something that should have killed the ninety nine forever.
It stopped making the penny. The last ones were struck at the Philadelphia Mint in November of twenty twenty five.
Each penny cost almost four cents to make which is a very strange way to run a one cent coin.
So think about it. If the penny is going away then nobody can hand you one cent in change. The ninety nine should be dead.
But it isn't dead. In September of twenty twenty six Congress passed a bill that lets stores round your cash total to the nearest nickel.
So if your total is nine ninety nine and you pay cash you hand over ten dollars. And if you tap your card you still pay nine ninety nine.
And the tag on the shelf still says nine ninety nine. The coin died and the trick didn't even blink.
Dave slumps on his couch and feels every one of his thirty something years. History couldn't explain it and honesty couldn't beat it and killing the penny couldn't stop it.
But then Dave notices one thing. The trick only works in the first second while your brain is on autopilot. So what if he grabbed the wheel?
Dave makes three small rules for himself. And remember that this is education and not advice.
Rule one is that he says every price out loud and rounds it up. Nineteen ninety nine becomes twenty. The cashier thinks he's weird and Dave does not care.
It sounds silly but it forces your brain to read the whole number and not just the first digit.
Rule two is that he keeps a running total in round numbers while he shops. No more mystery receipts.
Rule three is one question. Would I still want this at the round price? If a lamp is a yes at nineteen ninety nine and a no at twenty then you never wanted the lamp. You wanted the nine.
Then Dave knocks on Bob's door and says double or nothing.
Bob watches him shop. Dave mutters round numbers the whole way like a man counting sheep. At the exit he says one hundred and ten dollars.
The receipt says one hundred nine dollars and ninety four cents.
Bob pays up. Dave gets his twenty back and twenty more on top and for the first time he knows what he spent before the receipt does.
Now it's your turn because I made you a promise. Here's the exact tag from the first second of this video.
Read it out loud and round it up. It's four hundred dollars. If that's the first thing your brain said then the trick just stopped working on you.
So here's what Dave learned. Your brain reads the first digit and guesses the rest.
Nobody is sure who started the ninety nine and it outlived an honest store and a dead penny because it works on us.
And saying the round number out loud is enough to break it.
Oh and Dave finally said his real age out loud too. He's forty. He took it pretty well.
Next time Dave walks into a phone store and a very friendly salesman offers him a brand new phone for free. That should worry you.
Subscribe so the raccoon in the pricing office doesn't get you. It costs zero dollars. Not zero point nine nine. Zero.
